Müssen: obrigação e necessidade, passo a: Müssen: obligation and necessity, step by step
PASSO 1: «müssen» expressa o que você TE: STEP 1: «müssen» expresses what you HAVE TO do (obligation or necessity): «Ich muss arbeiten» = I have to work / I must work — "must" is its English cousin. STEP 2: conjugate: ich muss, du musst, er muss, wir müssen, ihr müsst, sie müssen. The «ü» disappears in the singular and, as with «können», «ich» and «er» are the same, with no -t. STEP 3: the second verb goes to the END, in the infinitive: «Du musst pünktlich sein.» STEP 4: question: «Muss ich heute arbeiten?» STEP 5: a separable verb stays WHOLE at the end: «Ich muss um sieben Uhr aufstehen.» English needs "have to" (two words plus "to"); German has one modal and no "to".
o português diz «ter que» (verbo ter + q: English says "I have to work" or "I must work". German only has the second pattern: «Ich muss arbeiten», with the infinitive at the end of the sentence. And remember the trap from lesson 11: «Ich muss nicht» means "I don't have to", not "I mustn't".
The whole infinitive goes to the end.

Wollen: querer, e a diferença para möcht: Wollen: want to, and how it differs from möchten
PASSO 1: «wollen» expressa uma vontade F: STEP 1: «wollen» expresses a FIRM wish or a plan: «Ich will nächste Woche nach Berlin fahren» = I want to go to Berlin next week. False friend alert: «ich will» never means "I will". STEP 2: conjugate: ich will, du willst, er will, wir wollen, ihr wollt, sie wollen. Careful: «ich» and «er» are both «will», with no -t. STEP 3: the infinitive goes to the end. STEP 4: «möchten» is softer and more polite ("I'd like"); «wollen» is direct ("I want"). When asking a stranger for something, prefer «möchten»: «Ich möchte einen Kaffee», not «Ich will einen Kaffee», which sounds curt — just like "I want a coffee" does in English.

PASSO 1: «dürfen» expressa PERMISSÃO: «D: STEP 1: «dürfen» expresses PERMISSION: «Darf ich hier sitzen?» = May I sit here? STEP 2: conjugate: ich darf, du darfst, er darf, wir dürfen, ihr dürft, sie dürfen (the «ü» disappears in the singular). STEP 3: with «nicht», «dürfen» means FORBIDDEN — it's the German "mustn't": «Hier darf man nicht rauchen» = you mustn't smoke here. STEP 4: «man» is impersonal, like English "one" or the general "you": «Hier darf man parken» (you can park here). It takes the «er» form of the verb. Signs use the infinitive or a noun: «Rauchen verboten», «Parken erlaubt», «Eingang», «Ausgang».
